1.title: Perito Moreno Glacier in a Day

periods.title: Los Glaciares National Park: First Views
periods.text: Depart El Calafate early (7–8am) for the 80km drive to Los Glaciares National Park. Most hostels arrange shared minibus transfers (ARS 15,000–25,000 return) or you can rent a car. The first glimpse of the glacier from the approach road is staggering: a 5km-wide wall of jagged blue ice rising 70 metres above Lago Argentino. Pay the park entry (ARS 25,000 for foreigners) and head straight to the boardwalks.
periods.tip: Book your transfer the evening before, as morning departures sell out in high season. Bring a packed lunch to avoid overpriced park cafeteria food.

periods.title: Boardwalks & Ice Calving
periods.text: Spend two to three hours on the extensive boardwalk network, where multiple platforms at different levels offer views of the glacier's northern face, southern face, and the Canal de los Témpanos where icebergs drift. The sound is extraordinary: deep groans, cracks like gunshots, and thunderous roars when house-sized chunks calve into the lake. The lower balconies put you closest to the ice wall. Pack layers, as wind off the glacier is fierce.
periods.tip: The best calving tends to happen in the afternoon when sun warms the ice face. Stay patient at the lower platforms, as you will witness ice falling if you wait.

periods.title: El Calafate: Patagonian Lamb
periods.text: Return to El Calafate by 6–7pm. Dinner on Avenida Libertador, the main strip lined with restaurants and bars. Try cordero patagónico (Patagonian lamb roasted over an open fire) at La Tablita or Casimiro Biguá (ARS 18,000–28,000). The lamb is slow-roasted for hours on a crucero (iron cross) and served with roast potatoes. Pair with a Patagonian Pinot Noir from Bodega del Fin del Mundo.
periods.tip: La Tablita fills up by 8:30pm, so arrive early or book ahead. The lamb for two is better value and more than enough food.

periods.title: El Calafate Town & Laguna Nimez
periods.text: Start with a walk along El Calafate's lakefront promenade on Lago Argentino, where the water is a milky turquoise from glacial sediment. Visit Laguna Nimez nature reserve (ARS 5,000) on the edge of town, a wetland sanctuary with flamingos, black-necked swans, and upland geese against a backdrop of snow-capped mountains. Breakfast at Borges y Álvarez Libro-Bar (ARS 5,000–8,000), a bookshop café.
periods.tip: Laguna Nimez is best at sunrise or late afternoon for bird photography. Flamingos are present from October to March during the austral summer.

periods.title: Glaciarium & Town Exploration
periods.text: Visit the Glaciarium (ARS 12,000), an excellent ice museum 6km from town explaining Patagonian glaciology, climate science, and the formation of the Southern Patagonian Ice Field. The ice bar inside serves drinks in glasses made of glacial ice (ARS 8,000 including a cocktail). Walk Avenida Libertador for outdoor gear shops, chocolate shops, and artisan craft stores selling guanaco wool products.
periods.tip: The Glaciarium shuttle runs from the town centre every two hours and is included in entry. The ice bar visit is timed, so book on arrival.

periods.title: Patagonian Dinner & Craft Beer
periods.text: Dinner at La Zaina (ARS 14,000–22,000) for creative Patagonian cuisine: smoked trout, wild boar, and calafate berry desserts. The calafate berry is the town's namesake, and legend says if you eat it, you will return to Patagonia. Drinks at Shackleton Bar for local craft beers (ARS 3,000–5,000 per pint) or La Zorra Taproom for Patagonian IPAs and stouts.
periods.tip: Try anything with calafate berry: ice cream, jam, beer, liqueur. The flavour is unique to this region and tastes like a mix of blueberry and blackcurrant.

periods.title: Glacier Approach & Upper Boardwalks
periods.text: Depart El Calafate at 8am for Los Glaciares National Park (80km, ARS 15,000–25,000 return transfer). Park entry is ARS 25,000 for foreigners, payable in cash or card at the gate. Start with the upper boardwalks for panoramic views. The glacier stretches 5km wide and 30km long, feeding into Lago Argentino. The ice is intensely blue in morning light, with deep crevasses and seracs (ice towers) visible from above.
periods.tip: Arrive before 10am to beat the tour bus crowds. The upper boardwalks are less crowded and offer the widest panoramic perspective of the entire glacier face.

periods.title: Lower Boardwalks & Ice Calving
periods.text: Descend to the lower boardwalks for close-up views of the glacier's towering ice wall, 70 metres of blue and white ice rising from the milky lake. This is where calving happens, with chunks ranging from refrigerator-sized to building-sized crashing into the water with deafening booms. The boardwalk system extends several kilometres with viewing platforms at multiple angles. Bring binoculars to spot condors and austral parakeets in the surrounding lenga forest.
periods.tip: Patience is everything for calving. Sit at the lower platforms for 30–45 minutes, as the deep cracking sounds warn you before a major collapse. Have your camera ready at all times.

periods.title: Lamb Asado & Stargazing
periods.text: Back in El Calafate, celebrate with cordero patagónico at La Tablita (ARS 18,000–28,000), lamb roasted on a crucero over open flames for four hours. Order the lamb shoulder for two with a bottle of Patagonian Malbec (ARS 6,000–12,000). After dinner, walk to the lakefront, where Patagonia's minimal light pollution makes for extraordinary stargazing. The Southern Cross is visible year-round.
periods.tip: The lamb at La Tablita or Don Pichón is slow-roasted and cannot be rushed. Order early if you are very hungry, as it takes time to prepare.

3.title: Mini-Trekking on the Ice or Boat Safari

periods.title: Mini-Trekking on Perito Moreno
periods.text: Book the mini-trekking experience (ARS 80,000–120,000 plus park entry, Hielo y Aventura operator), where a boat crosses the lake to the glacier base, then guides lead you onto the ice itself with crampons. Walk on blue ice ridges, peer into crevasses, and drink whisky chilled with thousand-year-old glacial ice. The trek lasts 90 minutes on the ice and is suitable for anyone with reasonable fitness. This is the highlight of Patagonia.
periods.tip: Book mini-trekking at least a week ahead in December–February. Wear hiking boots with ankle support, as crampons strap over them. No high heels or sandals.

periods.title: Boat Safari or Kayaking
periods.text: Take the Nautical Safari boat (ARS 30,000–45,000) that approaches the glacier's south face by water, where you see the full 70-metre ice wall from lake level, with icebergs floating around the boat. Alternatively, guided kayaking on Lago Argentino (ARS 40,000–60,000) paddles among icebergs within view of the glacier. Both options offer perspectives impossible from the boardwalks alone.
periods.tip: The boat safari is included in some mini-trekking packages. Check before booking separately. Kayaking requires moderate fitness and runs weather-dependent.

periods.title: Farewell Calafate
periods.text: Final evening in El Calafate. Dinner at Casimiro Biguá (ARS 16,000–26,000) for king crab (centolla) from Tierra del Fuego or Patagonian lamb ravioli. Walk the Avenida Libertador one last time and pick up calafate berry jam and Patagonian chocolate as souvenirs. End at Borges y Álvarez with a calafate berry gin and tonic and a good book about Patagonia.
periods.tip: Calafate berry products make excellent lightweight souvenirs. The artisan jam from local producers tastes far better than the commercial brands.

budgetTips.title: Blue dollar advantage
budgetTips.text: Bring US dollars in cash and exchange at the blue rate (roughly double the official rate). This makes Patagonia dramatically cheaper. Western Union also gives the blue rate. Never use ATMs or cards, as you lose 40–50% of value.

budgetTips.title: Pack your own food
budgetTips.text: Park cafeterias charge tourist prices. Buy empanadas, sandwiches, and snacks at La Anónima supermarket in El Calafate before heading to the glacier. A packed lunch saves ARS 10,000–15,000 per day.

budgetTips.title: Shared transfers
budgetTips.text: Shared minibuses to Perito Moreno cost ARS 15,000–25,000 return versus ARS 60,000+ for a private taxi. Book through your hostel or CalTur. For El Chaltén, the public bus is the cheapest option.

budgetTips.title: Free trails in El Chaltén
budgetTips.text: All trekking in El Chaltén is free, with no park entrance fee and no mandatory guides. The Fitz Roy and Torre trails are world-class and cost nothing. Only Perito Moreno National Park charges entry (ARS 25,000).

budgetTips.title: Cook at your hostel
budgetTips.text: Hostels in El Calafate and El Chaltén have kitchens. A steak and salad from the supermarket costs ARS 5,000–8,000 versus ARS 18,000–28,000 at a restaurant. Many travellers cook most nights and splurge once.

budgetTips.title: Book activities early
budgetTips.text: Mini-trekking and boat tours have fixed prices regardless of when you book, but they sell out weeks ahead in peak season. Booking early guarantees your spot. Last-minute availability is rare December through February.

budgetBreakdown.notes: Shared bus → private transfers → car rental
Boardwalks & free hikes → mini-trek → big ice & estancia
Supermarket wine → craft beer bars → restaurant wines

practicalInfo.title: Getting There
items: Fly to El Calafate Airport (FTE) from Buenos Aires (3 hours, Aerolíneas Argentinas or JetSmart). Book early, as prices surge in peak season
Airport shuttle to town: ARS 5,000 (20 minutes). Taxis: ARS 10,000–15,000. Most hostels can arrange pickup
From El Calafate, Perito Moreno Glacier is 80km (1.5 hours by shared transfer). El Chaltén is 220km north (3 hours by bus)

practicalInfo.title: Health & Safety
items: No vaccinations required. Tap water is safe. The main risks are sun exposure, wind chill, and dehydration, as Patagonian UV is intense even on cloudy days
Trails in El Chaltén are well-marked but weather changes fast. Carry rain gear, warm layers, and extra food on all hikes. Hypothermia is a real risk
Emergency: 911. El Calafate has a small hospital. Travel insurance with helicopter evacuation coverage is recommended for trekking

practicalInfo.title: What to Pack
items: Windproof and waterproof outer layer, because Patagonian wind is brutal and constant. Even summer days can feel cold on the glacier boardwalks
Hiking boots with ankle support (mandatory for mini-trekking). Thermal base layers, fleece mid-layer, warm hat, and gloves
Sunscreen SPF 50+, UV-blocking sunglasses, and a buff or balaclava for wind protection. Binoculars for wildlife and ice details

practicalInfo.title: Connectivity
items: WiFi in El Calafate hotels and cafes is reliable. El Chaltén WiFi is slower and patchy. No signal at the glacier or on trails
Download offline maps (Google Maps or Maps.me) before heading to the park. Cell coverage is spotty outside towns
Personal or Movistar SIM cards work in El Calafate but coverage drops to zero in the national park and on the road to El Chaltén

practicalInfo.title: Money
items: BRING US DOLLARS IN CASH. Blue dollar rate in El Calafate gives roughly double the official rate. Exchange at your hostel or local shops
Cards accepted at most restaurants and tour operators but charged at the official rate, so always prefer cash. ATMs exist but have low limits and high fees
Tip 10% at restaurants (not included). Tipping tour guides ARS 3,000–5,000 per person for a day trip is appreciated

practicalInfo.title: Best Time to Visit
items: October to March (austral spring/summer) has the longest days and warmest weather (5–15°C). December to February is peak season
March and April offer autumn colours, fewer crowds, and still-decent weather. May to September is cold, dark, and many services close
Weather is unpredictable year-round, so pack for four seasons in one day. Wind is the constant and it rarely stops in Patagonia

culturalTips.title: Patagonian Lamb
culturalTips.text: Cordero patagónico is roasted for hours on a crucero (iron cross) over open wood fire. The meat falls off the bone with a smoky, tender flavour unlike any lamb you have tasted. Order it whenever you see a crucero outside a restaurant, as it means they are cooking the real thing.

culturalTips.title: Mate in the Wind
culturalTips.text: Mate is Argentina's social ritual, shared from a gourd with a metal bombilla straw. In Patagonia, drinking mate in howling wind is practically a sport. If offered, accept. Say gracias only when you want to stop. Never stir the bombilla.

culturalTips.title: Respect the Wind
culturalTips.text: Patagonian wind is not weather. It is a force of nature. It can knock you off balance, blow away unsecured gear, and change the temperature by 10°C in minutes. Locals live with it and never complain. Secure everything and always carry a windproof layer.

culturalTips.title: Leave No Trace
culturalTips.text: Patagonian trails operate on strict leave-no-trace principles. Carry all rubbish out, stay on marked paths, do not light fires outside designated areas, and camp only in official sites. Park rangers actively enforce these rules and will fine violators.

culturalTips.title: Condor Watching
culturalTips.text: The Andean condor, the world's largest flying bird with a 3-metre wingspan, soars over both El Calafate and El Chaltén. Look up at cliff edges and thermal updrafts, especially in the morning. Seeing one ride the wind silently is a defining Patagonian moment.

culturalTips.title: Patagonian Pace
culturalTips.text: Things move slowly in Patagonia. Buses leave when full, restaurants cook when ready, and weather dictates everything. Fighting this leads to frustration. Embrace the slow pace, carry a book, and remember that you came here to disconnect from speed.
